posts.note: Cigna/Evernorth dTMS-for-OCD coverage news. Includes a quoted Cigna policy statement the author adopts, two own-publication commitments, a replication-size call, a Nobel-candidates aside, a joking image aside, and a footnote durability claim.
HIPAA/post-Dobbs privacy essay. Mostly present-tense legal analysis and satire (Coke thought experiment); two borderline forward-looking generalizations about state lawmakers logged.
Short thread post; two enforcement-wave forecasts (coming enforcement crisis; CAA fiduciary-duty enforcement).
Argument that TMS should be first-line for severe depression. Title is a question; all calls are 'should' statements with no predictive reading; nothing logged.

Self-published survey paper (300 clinicians, Feb-Mar 2020 data) with co-author Carlene MacMillan. Forecasts cluster in the Discussion (insurance-enablement platforms: Alma, Grow Therapy, Talkspace, BetterHelp) and in the Solutions/Conclusions sections (value-based care, enforcement, at-risk contracting). Pure 'should' sentences not logged.

statements.quote: Cigna will be issuing an updated revision to its TMS medical coverage policy effective September 15, 2022, extending coverage to patients aged 18 and older diagnosed with OCD.
statements.context: Quoted Cigna/Evernorth announcement reproduced by the author as the news of the post: Cigna revises its TMS medical coverage policy to cover deep TMS for OCD in adults 18 and older, effective 2022-09-15, one day after the post date. The author endorses and celebrates it ('Evernorth, formerly CIGNA, now covers dTMS for OCD!').
statements.note: Quoted third-party (Cigna) policy text; author adopts it. Announced decision, effective one day after the post.

statements.quote: Further data is coming, but we know that greater than half of patients (58%) with treatment resistant OCD (trOCD) get a 30% or greater reduction in symptoms.
statements.context: After the coverage news, the author says more data on deep TMS (BrainsWay H7 coil) for treatment-resistant OCD is coming, alongside the present 58% response figure from post-marketing data.
statements.note: Only 'Further data is coming' is forward-looking; the 58% figure is a present claim.

statements.quote: We are publishing, in the future, an open label data, demonstrating that around 20% of patients can get to remission of their OCD symptoms.
statements.context: The author says his group (former practice, Evernorth partnership, BrainsWay collaborators) will publish open-label data showing about 20% of treatment-resistant OCD patients reach remission with deep TMS.
statements.note: Own-publication commitment with a numeric claim (about 20% remission); coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: This data needs to be replicated in sham controlled studies, but likely not large ones.
statements.context: On accelerated deep TMS for OCD (20% remission in five days, likened to Stanford SAINT): the author expects replication in sham-controlled studies will not need large trials because placebo response in treatment-resistant OCD is very low.
statements.note: Compound: normative 'needs to be replicated' plus a prediction that the replication studies will not need to be large.

statements.quote: Between Dr. Nolan Williams at Stanford and Drs. Abraham Zangen and Aron Tendler ... I think we have a few Nobel Prize candidates in psychiatry again, finally!
statements.context: Aside about the SAINT (Stanford) and BrainsWay deep TMS researchers; the author calls them Nobel Prize candidates.
statements.note: Implicit forecast: 'candidates', not a call that they will win. Borderline; footnote marker 22 skipped with the join.

statements.quote: Although, honestly, in the future, I may just use this graphic:
statements.context: Joking aside about an image the author may reuse in future newsletter posts, after a mismatched-picture gag about the SAINT trial data.
statements.note: Joking aside about the newsletter's own images; no forecast value. Logged for completeness.

statements.quote: You will remember "having fewer OCD symptoms" for a while, but not forever, probably.
statements.context: Footnote 15, explaining brain stimulation: repeated TMS sessions teach the brain like flash cards; the benefit (fewer OCD symptoms) lasts a while but probably not forever. Generic clinical durability claim addressed to a hypothetical patient.
statements.horizon_text: for a while, but not forever
statements.note: Generic clinical claim about durability of TMS benefit; borderline forward-looking.

statements.quote: So any state can pass any law in the absence of a federal right to privacy in which they now have a government interest in law-enforcement of. And if there is no limit on the laws they can pass that invade our privacy, literally any law passed can allow the government to access our health information.
statements.context: After listing HIPAA's 12 national-priority disclosure purposes, the author argues that after the overturn of Roe v. Wade, with no federal privacy right, states can pass laws that let government reach protected health information through HIPAA's law-enforcement exceptions (Texas and abortion-banning states given as examples; 'If you're an enemy of the state and you're being investigated, there's no reason they can't review your therapist documentation').
statements.note: Capability claim ('can') about future state laws; borderline between present legal analysis and forecast.

statements.quote: There is no law so invasive or punitive that lawmakers will demure if it comes to controlling either doctors or women. Preferably both.
statements.context: Reacting to a headline seen the morning of writing; the author predicts lawmakers will not shy away from any invasive or punitive law that controls doctors or women (abortion-enforcement context).
statements.note: Rhetorical generalization about future legislative behavior; near-truism.

statements.quote: Some of you have been following my series of arguments about the coming enforcement crisis/opportunity in Healthcare.
statements.context: Opening of a short thread post about the Texas Attorney General avoiding a subpoena. The author refers to his running thesis that a healthcare enforcement crisis/opportunity is coming, triggered by the overturn of Roe v. Wade and fiduciary-duty clarifications.
statements.note: Restatement of an earlier series thesis.

statements.quote: I also believe there will be a tidal wave of enforcement coming with the passage of the Combined Appropriations Act of 2020 and its clarification of the fiduciary duty of plan sponsors and brokers when it comes to health benefits and the like.
statements.context: The author predicts a wave of enforcement actions following the Consolidated Appropriations Act (he writes 'Combined Appropriations Act of 2020') and its fiduciary-duty clarifications for health plan sponsors and brokers. He cites DOJ suing Idaho over EMTALA and a Department of Labor amicus brief in Massachusetts on Blue Cross Blue Shield fiduciary duty as early signs.
statements.confidence_phrase: I also believe there will be
entities: Consolidated Appropriations Act (author: Combined Appropriations Act of 2020)
statements.note: Payer/employer-plan fiduciary enforcement; area could also be payer_policy.

statements.quote: People were, and are, starting companies left and right based around the hypothesis that making the process of taking insurance easier is going to lead to a great company, but no data exists to support the fundamental hypothesis that mental health professionals want to take insurance in one particular way or another.
statements.context: Opening of the self-published survey paper on clinician attitudes toward insurance. The forecast ('is going to lead to a great company') belongs to startup founders and investors; the author disputes its evidence base and argues against it later in the Discussion.
statements.note: Third-party hypothesis the author does not adopt; his own contrary calls appear in the Discussion section.

statements.quote: It does not mean that it will be submitted in some unbelievably stale format to JAMA Psychiatry, or any of the other journals that would give it prestige
statements.context: The author explains he will publish the insurance-attitudes study in the newsletter and will not submit it to JAMA Psychiatry or other academic journals.
statements.confidence_phrase: does not mean that it will be
statements.note: Own-activity negative call about publication venue; low forecast value; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: The most important truth is that, for mental health conditions, a system that is stressful, feels controlling, and underpays you by a factor of many multiples of what you could be making otherwise is not a sustainable business model for clinicians.
statements.context: Discussion section of the survey paper (300 clinicians; 98% report stress dealing with insurers; 27% resigned from panels). The author claims the insurance fee-for-service model is not sustainable for mental health clinicians.
statements.note: Sustainability claim; implicit forecast that clinicians will keep leaving insurance panels.

statements.quote: Thus, the endless platform solutions that are doing clinicians a service by making it easier to take insurance are in for, possibly, a really harsh awakening unless they can change the way payers value the mental health clinicians in their network.
statements.context: Discussion: insurance-enablement platforms for therapists (the author names Alma, Grow Therapy, Talkspace and BetterHelp in the next paragraph) face a harsh awakening unless payers change how they value in-network mental health clinicians.
statements.note: Conditional ('unless'). Company names appear in the following paragraph.

statements.quote: Paying a few dollars more per claim is not going to cut it.
statements.context: Same Discussion passage; the author predicts small per-claim reimbursement increases will not fix clinician attrition from insurance networks.

statements.quote: This is a serious problem for the business models of all clinicians who take insurance and all mental health platforms. I'm looking at you Alma. I'm looking at you, Grow Therapy. This extends, of course, to Talk Space, Better Help, etc.
statements.context: The author names the platforms whose business models depend on therapists taking insurance: Alma, Grow Therapy, Talkspace, BetterHelp. Their path to scale is insurance; the survey data says clinicians' path to success is to leave insurance panels.
statements.note: Present-tense assessment with a forward implication for the named companies; companion to the 'harsh awakening' call.

statements.quote: These force clinicians to take insurance as service platforms haven't been around long enough to have their panels of therapists all quit.
statements.context: Implicit prediction that, given enough time, therapists on insurance-enablement platforms (Alma, Grow Therapy, etc.) will quit their panels, as 27% of surveyed clinicians already resigned from insurance panels. Author calls the platforms' model a bait and switch.
statements.note: Implicit forecast (therapists will quit the platforms in time). Reads as 'force-clinicians-to-take-insurance-as-a-service platforms'.

statements.quote: Maybe these platform solutions will do a better job of negotiating those contracts, but it's not that much better.
statements.context: On insurance rates paid to therapists (called absurd; a $7 group-therapy rate; under $100 per session typical): platforms may negotiate somewhat better payer contracts, but not much better.
statements.note: Hedged; the second clause is present tense but concerns the platforms' negotiated rates.

statements.quote: A bunch of different companies scrambling to get pieces of that limited pie is going to make for a couple of exits, but it's not gonna change healthcare.
statements.context: Therapist time is a non-scalable, limited resource (45- or 60-minute blocks); the author predicts the platform race will produce a couple of company exits but will not change healthcare.
statements.note: Two-part claim: some exits will happen; healthcare will not change.

statements.quote: And therapists are going to quit. And then they're going to go back to doing less scalable work, and everyone's gonna be worse off.
statements.context: Continuation of the exits claim: therapists on insurance platforms will quit and return to less scalable (private-pay) work, leaving everyone worse off.
statements.note: Clinician-behavior forecast tied to the platform calls; area could also be company_market.

statements.quote: And arbitrage on the difference between what we therapists think is nice and what people are actually worth is a fine strategy for a company until it's not.
statements.context: Platforms profit from therapists' willingness to accept low fees (sliding scales); the author predicts this arbitrage strategy works only until it stops working.
statements.note: Near-truism ('works until it doesn't'); implicit forecast that the strategy fails.

statements.quote: Training in fundamentals of payment systems could help clinicians navigate the insurance system. Still, this would not address frustrations related to bureaucratic friction and low reimbursement.
statements.context: Discussion of work settings (70% of respondents said to feel incapable of dealing with insurance; the Results section earlier gives 22% incapable, 65% capable). Conditional claim about the effect of payment-systems training.
statements.note: Conditional/hypothetical intervention effect; weak forecast.

statements.quote: Moreover, in order to win back mental health clinicians, insurance providers must offer solutions to address the poor reimbursement and administrative burden that drives clinicians into the private pay market.
statements.context: Solutions section of the paper. Conditional predictive reading: clinicians will not return to insurance panels unless payers fix reimbursement and administrative burden.
statements.note: 'Must' sentence with a conditional predictive reading (no return of clinicians without payer changes).

statements.quote: Additionally, enforcement of existing laws that regulate mental health parity, prompt payment, and other statutes would make the adversarial attitude sometimes encountered by clinicians less "hazard free" for payers.
statements.context: Proposed systemic solution: enforcement of mental health parity and prompt-payment laws would raise the cost to payers of adversarial behavior toward clinicians.
statements.note: Conditional forecast about the effect of enforcement; ties to the author's enforcement-wave thesis.

statements.quote: The opportunity for behavioral health providers who are willing to go "at risk" and work in teams that approximate the acuity managed by IOP/PHP/some inpatient providers is coming.
statements.context: Solutions section: the author predicts at-risk (value-based) contracting opportunities will come for outpatient behavioral health teams that manage IOP/PHP-level acuity, especially with self-funded employers; providers need to be ready.
statements.note: Followed by the normative 'Our providers need to be ready'. Relevant to the author's own at-risk ventures; coder may consider CONTROL.

statements.quote: We see a shift towards shared-risk, value-based care as a way to reduce the stress clinicians experience interacting with insurance providers.
statements.context: Solutions section, authors' voice (Muir, MacMillan and co-authors): they see a shift toward shared-risk value-based care and expect it to reduce clinician stress with insurers.
statements.note: Trend observation with a forward expectation; borderline.

statements.quote: Value-based care would assist in reducing the contentious relations between mental health providers and insurance companies.
statements.context: Conclusions of the paper; conditional forecast about value-based care's effect on provider-payer relations.
statements.note: Conditional ('would'); restates the shared-risk expectation.
